claim: TBC1D3 is a hominoid-specific gene that undergoes segmental duplications during hominoid evolution.
source: The hominoid-specific gene TBC1D3 undergoes segmental duplications during hominoid evolution, but its role in brain development has not been explored.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature establishing TBC1D3's evolutionary origin and duplication pattern.

claim: Expression of TBC1D3 in ventricular cortical progenitors of mice via in utero electroporation causes delamination of ventricular radial glia cells (vRGs).
source: Here, we found that expression of TBC1D3 in ventricular cortical progenitors of mice via in utero electroporation caused delamination of ventricular radial glia cells (vRGs) and promoted generation of self-renewing basal progenitors with typical morphology of outer radial glia (oRG), which are most abundant in primates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in utero electroporation experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: Expression of TBC1D3 promotes generation of self-renewing basal progenitors with typical morphology of outer radial glia (oRG).
source: Here, we found that expression of TBC1D3 in ventricular cortical progenitors of mice via in utero electroporation caused delamination of ventricular radial glia cells (vRGs) and promoted generation of self-renewing basal progenitors with typical morphology of outer radial glia (oRG), which are most abundant in primates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations including morphological analysis and marker expression.

claim: Outer radial glia (oRG) are most abundant in primates.
source: Here, we found that expression of TBC1D3 in ventricular cortical progenitors of mice via in utero electroporation caused delamination of ventricular radial glia cells (vRGs) and promoted generation of self-renewing basal progenitors with typical morphology of outer radial glia (oRG), which are most abundant in primates.
evidence: This is established knowledge from comparative neurobiology studies.

claim: Down-regulation of TBC1D3 in cultured human brain slices decreases generation of oRGs.
source: Furthermore, down-regulation of TBC1D3 in cultured human brain slices decreased generation of oRGs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments in human brain slices.

claim: Localized oRG proliferation resulting from in utero electroporation of TBC1D3 underlies cortical regions exhibiting folding.
source: Interestingly, localized oRG proliferation resulting from either in utero electroporation or transgenic expression of TBC1D3, was often found to underlie cortical regions exhibiting folding.
evidence: This is based on observational data from electroporated and transgenic mice.

claim: Localized oRG proliferation resulting from transgenic expression of TBC1D3 underlies cortical regions exhibiting folding.
source: Interestingly, localized oRG proliferation resulting from either in utero electroporation or transgenic expression of TBC1D3, was often found to underlie cortical regions exhibiting folding.
evidence: This is based on observational data from transgenic mice.

claim: TBC1D3 is required for oRG generation in regulating cortical expansion and folding.
source: Thus, we have identified a hominoid gene that is required for oRG generation in regulating the cortical expansion and folding.
evidence: This conclusion is based on both gain-of-function (mouse) and loss-of-function (human) experiments.

claim: The expansion of the mammalian neocortex during evolution correlates with the increase in intelligence.
source: It is generally assumed that the expansion of the mammalian neocortex during evolution correlates with the increase in intelligence, and this process involves increased production of cortical neurons, resulting from an extended neurogenic period as well as increased proliferative ability of neural stem cells and progenitors (Geschwind and Rakic, 2013; Lui et al., 2011; Sun and Hevner, 2014; Zilles et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a general assumption in the field supported by cited literature.

claim: Cortical expansion involves increased production of cortical neurons resulting from an extended neurogenic period and increased proliferative ability of neural stem cells and progenitors.
source: It is generally assumed that the expansion of the mammalian neocortex during evolution correlates with the increase in intelligence, and this process involves increased production of cortical neurons, resulting from an extended neurogenic period as well as increased proliferative ability of neural stem cells and progenitors (Geschwind and Rakic, 2013; Lui et al., 2011; Sun and Hevner, 2014; Zilles et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on cortical development.

claim: Expanded cortical surfaces are folded to form gyri and sulci to fit into a limited cranium.
source: To fit into a limited cranium, expanded cortical surfaces are folded to form gyri and sulci.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about brain structure.

claim: An outer subventricular zone (OSVZ) emerges in the primate cortex, consisting of a massive pool of proliferating basal progenitors (BPs) and post-mitotic neurons.
source: Recent cross-species studies have shown the emergence of an outer subventricular zone (OSVZ) in the primate cortex, consisting of a massive pool of proliferating basal progenitors (BPs) and post-mitotic neurons (Betizeau et al., 2013; Fietz et al., 2010; Hansen et al., 2010; Reillo et al., 2011; Smart et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by cited cross-species comparative studies.

claim: Ventricular radial glial cells are neuroepithelia-derived and undergo repeated and typically asymmetric cell division at the apical surface of the ventricular zone.
source: Unlike the neuroepithelia-derived ventricular radial glial cells, which undergo repeated and typically asymmetric cell division at the apical surface of the ventricular zone, the BPs, after delamination from the apical surface, translocate to the SVZ, where they exhibit symmetric or asymmetric divisions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neural progenitor cell behavior.

claim: Basal progenitors (BPs) delaminate from the apical surface and translocate to the SVZ where they exhibit symmetric or asymmetric divisions.
source: Unlike the neuroepithelia-derived ventricular radial glial cells, which undergo repeated and typically asymmetric cell division at the apical surface of the ventricular zone, the BPs, after delamination from the apical surface, translocate to the SVZ, where they exhibit symmetric or asymmetric divisions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about basal progenitor behavior.

claim: In primates, outer radial glia (oRG) and intermediate progenitors (IPs) in the OSVZ are two major forms of BPs.
source: In primates, the recently identified outer (basal) radial glia (referred to as oRG or bRG) and the intermediate progenitors (IPs) in the OSVZ, which can undergo multiple rounds of symmetric or asymmetric divisions (Betizeau et al., 2013; Hansen et al., 2010), are two major forms of BPs.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on primate brain development.

claim: Primate oRG and IPs can undergo multiple rounds of symmetric or asymmetric divisions.
source: In primates, the recently identified outer (basal) radial glia (referred to as oRG or bRG) and the intermediate progenitors (IPs) in the OSVZ, which can undergo multiple rounds of symmetric or asymmetric divisions (Betizeau et al., 2013; Hansen et al., 2010), are two major forms of BPs.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on primate neural progenitors.

claim: IPs and minimal oRG cells in the mouse SVZ usually exhibit final division to generate a pair of post-mitotic neurons.
source: By contrast, the IPs and minimal oRG cells in the mouse SVZ usually exhibit final division to generate a pair of post-mitotic neurons (Shitamukai et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on mouse neural progenitors.

claim: The radial and lateral expansion of BPs is thought to be a main cause of cortical folding of gyrencephalic species.
source: The radial and lateral expansion of BPs is thought to be a main cause of cortical folding of gyrencephalic species (Fietz and Huttner, 2011; Fietz et al., 2010; Hansen et al., 2010; Lewitus et al., 2014; Lui et al., 2011; Reillo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: Forced expansion of BPs by down-regulating Trnp1 results in gyrification of the cerebral cortex in naturally lissencephalic mouse.
source: In support of this hypothesis, forced expansion of BPs by down-regulating the DNA-associated protein Trnp1 or overexpressing cell cycle regulatory proteins Cdk4/Cyclin D1 resulted in gyrification of the cerebral cortex in naturally lissencephalic mouse or gyrencephalic ferret (Nonaka-Kinoshita et al., 2013; Stahl et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited experimental studies.

claim: Overexpressing cell cycle regulatory proteins Cdk4/Cyclin D1 results in gyrification of the cerebral cortex in gyrencephalic ferret.
source: In support of this hypothesis, forced expansion of BPs by down-regulating the DNA-associated protein Trnp1 or overexpressing cell cycle regulatory proteins Cdk4/Cyclin D1 resulted in gyrification of the cerebral cortex in naturally lissencephalic mouse or gyrencephalic ferret (Nonaka-Kinoshita et al., 2013; Stahl et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited experimental studies.

claim: TBC1D3 paralogues are expressed in most human tissues, including the brain.
source: A previous study showed that TBC1D3 paralogues are expressed in most human tissues, including the brain (Hodzic et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a cited previous study.

claim: The expression of TBC1D3 in the fetal human brain (gestational week 26 to 40) is higher than that in the adult.
source: By using reverse transcription PCR, we found that the expression of TBC1D3 in the fetal human brain (gestational week, GW 26 to 40) was higher than that in the adult (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TBC1D3 shows high expression near the ventricular surface and in the subventricular zone of GW18 human cortical sections.
source: Immunofluorescence staining of cortical sections obtained from GW18 human specimens during the peak period of neurogenesis revealed high TBC1D3 expression near the ventricular surface and in the subventricular zone (SVZ) (Figure 1B), suggesting a role of TBC1D3 in cortex development.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Expression of TBC1D3 causes a decreased level of N-cadherin at adherens junctions at the ventricular surface.
source: Interestingly, expression of TBC1D3 caused delamination of ventricular radial glia (vRG), and a decreased level of N-cadherin at adherens junctions (AJs) (Figure 1D) at the ventricular surface.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The reduction in N-cadherin is due to either transcriptional inhibition or destabilization of transcripts.
source: The reduction in N-cadherin was probably due to either the transcriptional inhibition or destabilization of transcripts, because in situ hybridization and real-time PCR showed marked reduction of N-cadherin (Cdh2) transcript in VZ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and flow cytometry-sorted YFP+ cells expressing TBC1D3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization and real-time PCR data.

claim: Expression of TBC1D3 causes destabilization of Cdh2 mRNA in ReNeuron human neural progenitor cell line.
source: Further analyses showed that expression of TBC1D3 indeed caused destabilization of Cdh2 mRNA in ReNeuron human neural progenitor cell line (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by mRNA stability assay data.

claim: N-cadherin is important for maintaining the alignment of radial glial cells at VZ.
source: Since N-cadherin is known to be important for maintaining the alignment of radial glial cells at VZ (Kadowaki et al., 2007), reduction of N-cadherin due to TBC1D3 expression may be causally related to the delamination of ventricular neuroprogenitors.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: Reduction of N-cadherin due to TBC1D3 expression may be causally related to the delamination of ventricular neuroprogenitors.
source: Since N-cadherin is known to be important for maintaining the alignment of radial glial cells at VZ (Kadowaki et al., 2007), reduction of N-cadherin due to TBC1D3 expression may be causally related to the delamination of ventricular neuroprogenitors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed N-cadherin reduction and delamination.

claim: Expression of TBC1D3 causes dislocalization of Numb and integrin beta 1 (ITGB1) which were originally polarized in endfeet of vRGs.
source: Indeed, we found that expression of TBC1D3 caused dislocalization of Numb and integrin beta 1 (ITGB1) which were originally polarized distributed in endfeet of vRGs (Campos et al., 2004; Katayama et al., 2011; Rasin et al., 2007), without disrupting the junction integrity of the VZ as revealed by actin filaments (F-actin) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression of TBC1D3 does not disrupt the junction integrity of the VZ as revealed by actin filaments.
source: Indeed, we found that expression of TBC1D3 caused dislocalization of Numb and integrin beta 1 (ITGB1) which were originally polarized distributed in endfeet of vRGs (Campos et al., 2004; Katayama et al., 2011; Rasin et al., 2007), without disrupting the junction integrity of the VZ as revealed by actin filaments (F-actin) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by F-actin staining data.

claim: Delaminated TBC1D3-expressing cells often exhibit clustered distribution by forming vertical column-like structures in the SVZ and IZ of E16.5 mice.
source: Observation in the SVZ and intermediate zone (IZ) of E16.5 mice (electroporated at E13.5) showed that delaminated TBC1D3-expressing cells often exhibited clustered distribution by forming vertical column-like structures (Figure 1E), reminiscent of ontogenic radial units (Rakic, 1988), expansion of which has been proposed to underlie cortical folding (Borrell and Gotz, 2014; Florio and Huttner, 2014; Lui et al., 2011; Rakic, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 1E.

claim: Column-like aggregation of basal cells induced by TBC1D3 expression may result from increased number of proliferating cells originated from VZ.
source: This column-like aggregation of basal cells induced by TBC1D3 expression may result from increased number of proliferating cells originated from VZ (see below), and leads to lateral heterogeneity in the rate of neuronal production that may contribute to cortical folding.
evidence: This is an inference based on observed cell distribution patterns.

claim: Column-like aggregation of basal cells leads to lateral heterogeneity in the rate of neuronal production that may contribute to cortical folding.
source: This column-like aggregation of basal cells induced by TBC1D3 expression may result from increased number of proliferating cells originated from VZ (see below), and leads to lateral heterogeneity in the rate of neuronal production that may contribute to cortical folding.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of cortical folding.

claim: Disruption of AJs due to the loss of RhoA in neural progenitors is accompanied by an elevated proliferation of neuroprogenitors.
source: Previous studies have shown that disruption of AJs due to the loss of RhoA in neural progenitors is accompanied by an elevated proliferation of neuroprogenitors (Katayama et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited previous studies.

claim: TBC1D3 expression causes an increase in BrdU-positive proliferating cells compared to control mice.
source: We found that TBC1D3 expression caused an increase in BrdU-positive (BrdU+) proliferating cells, as compared to that of control mice electroporated with vehicle construct (Figure 2C,E).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation data shown in Figure 2C,E.

claim: Expressing a mutated form of TBC1D3 with deletion of amino acids 286 to 353 has no effect on BrdU incorporation.
source: In an additional control experiment, we found that expressing a mutated form of TBC1D3, with the deletion of amino acids 286 to 353 (∆286–353) essential for its cytoplasmic retention (He et al., 2014), in neural progenitors had no effect on BrdU incorporation (Figure 2C,E).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation data with the mutant construct.

claim: Cytoplasmic presence of TBC1D3 promotes the proliferation of early neural precursors.
source: These results suggest that cytoplasmic presence of TBC1D3 promotes the proliferation of early neural precursors.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of wild-type and mutant TBC1D3 effects.

claim: TBC1D3 expression causes BrdU+ cells to scatter widely across the cortex from VZ to CP, with the highest concentration in SVZ.
source: Interestingly, the TBC1D3-induced population of BrdU+ cells scattered widely across the cortex, from VZ to CP, with the highest concentration in SVZ (Figure 2B,C,F), indicating increased generation of BPs.
evidence: This is supported by BrdU distribution data shown in Figure 2B,C,F.

claim: The basal localized BrdU+ cells are basal progenitors (BPs) as revealed by positive Ki67 and negative NeuN labeling.
source: The identity of these basal localized cells as BPs was further revealed by positive labeling by Ki67, a marker for cells in cell cycle, and negative labeling by NeuN, a marker for post-mitotic neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by double-labeling immunostaining data.

claim: TBC1D3 expression causes an increase in the proportion of PH3+ cells in basal regions and a decrease in cells attached to the ventricular surface.
source: This effect of TBC1D3 expression was also confirmed by the increase in the proportion of cells stained with the mitotic marker phosphorylated Histone (PH3+) in basal regions and a decrease in cells attached to the ventricular surface (Figure 2D,G).
evidence: This is supported by PH3 staining data shown in Figure 2D,G.

claim: Electroporation with pCAGGS-TBC1D3-IRES-EGFP causes increase in numbers of basal BrdU+ or PH3+ cells in EGFP+ but not in EGFP- cells.
source: The seemingly non-cell autonomous effect of TBC1D3 expression on proliferation of BPs was most likely caused by different dosages of pE/nestin-TBC1D3 and pCAG-YFP (3:1) used in electroporation, because electroporation with pCAGGS-TBC1D3-IRES-EGFP, a vector co-expressing both TBC1D3 and EGFP, caused increase in numbers of basal BrdU+ or PH3+ cells in EGFP+ but not in EGFP- cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by cell-autonomous analysis data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The increase in PH3+ BPs is largely abolished when TBC1D3 and N-cadherin are co-expressed in neuroprogenitors.
source: We found that the increase in PH3+ BPs was largely abolished when TBC1D3 and N-cadherin were co-expressed in neuroprogenitors via in utero electroporation (Figure 2D,G), consistent with the contribution of delamination to the increased number of proliferating BPs.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2D,G.

claim: Delamination itself is not sufficient to transform vRG to BPs.
source: To determine whether delamination itself is sufficient to transform vRG to BPs, we over-expressed in vRG the extracellular domain (EC1) of N-cadherin, which has been shown to be capable of disrupting the homophilic intercellular N-cadherin interaction (Tan et al., 2010), and found that EC1 expression caused detachment of vRG cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B) but had no effect on the proliferation of either apical or basal cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–F). Thus, detachment of vRG cells is a necessary but not a sufficient step for the generation of proliferative BPs.
evidence: This is supported by EC1 overexpression experiment data.

claim: Detachment of vRG cells is a necessary but not sufficient step for the generation of proliferative BPs.
source: To determine whether delamination itself is sufficient to transform vRG to BPs, we over-expressed in vRG the extracellular domain (EC1) of N-cadherin, which has been shown to be capable of disrupting the homophilic intercellular N-cadherin interaction (Tan et al., 2010), and found that EC1 expression caused detachment of vRG cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B) but had no effect on the proliferation of either apical or basal cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–F). Thus, detachment of vRG cells is a necessary but not a sufficient step for the generation of proliferative BPs.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the EC1 experiment results.

claim: TBC1D3 has been shown to promote cell proliferation.
source: TBC1D3 has been shown to promote cell proliferation (Pei et al., 2002), activate Ras and enhance EGF/EGFR and insulin signaling in non-neuronal cells (Wainszelbaum et al., 2008, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited previous studies.

claim: TBC1D3 activates Ras and enhances EGF/EGFR and insulin signaling in non-neuronal cells.
source: TBC1D3 has been shown to promote cell proliferation (Pei et al., 2002), activate Ras and enhance EGF/EGFR and insulin signaling in non-neuronal cells (Wainszelbaum et al., 2008, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited previous studies.

claim: The effect of TBC1D3 on the proliferation of BPs is markedly abrogated by co-expression with RasS17N (Ras-DN), a dominant-negative form of Ras.
source: In line with this notion, we found that the effect of TBC1D3 on the proliferation of BPs was markedly abrogated by co-expression with RasS17N (Ras-DN), a dominant-negative form of Ras (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by Ras-DN co-expression experiment data.

claim: Ras signaling is involved in the proliferation of TBC1D3-induced BPs.
source: This result suggests the involvement of Ras signaling in the proliferation of TBC1D3-induced BPs, indicating multiple actions of TBC1D3 in causing increased expansion of BPs.
evidence: This is inferred from the Ras-DN rescue experiment.

claim: Intermediate progenitors (IPs) that express Tbr2 in the SVZ are the major type of BPs in mice.
source: In mice, intermediate progenitors (IPs) that express the transcription factor Tbr2 in the SVZ are the major type of BPs, which undergo terminal division (Lui et al., 2011; Noctor et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: Mouse IPs undergo terminal division.
source: In mice, intermediate progenitors (IPs) that express the transcription factor Tbr2 in the SVZ are the major type of BPs, which undergo terminal division (Lui et al., 2011; Noctor et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: Highly proliferative oRG cells are thought to be critical for the expansion of primate brain cerebral cortex.
source: Highly proliferative oRG cells are thought to be critical for the expansion of primate brain cerebral cortex (Hansen et al., 2010; Sun and Hevner, 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by cited literature.

claim: TBC1D3 expression causes an increase in Pax6+ cells in the mouse cortex, especially in the basal regions.
source: Remarkably, we found that TBC1D3 expression caused an increase in Pax6+ cells in the mouse cortex, especially in the basal regions (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by Pax6 immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: Many Sox2+ or Pax6+ BPs in TBC1D3-expressing mouse cortical slices exhibit a single process pointing to the pial surface with intense signals of mitosis-specific phospho-Vimentin (p-Vim).
source: In TBC1D3-expressing mouse cortical slices, we observed that many Sox2+ or Pax6+ BPs exhibited a single process pointing to the pial surface with intense signals of mitosis-specific phospho-Vimentin (p-Vim) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D), similar to unipolar oRGs identified in the human fetal brain (Fietz et al., 2010; Hansen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: In control mice, the percentage of Sox2+/p-Vim+ or Pax6+/p-Vim+ cells with a basal process is much lower than in TBC1D3-expressing mice.
source: However, in control mice, the percentage of Sox2+/p-Vim+ or Pax6+/p-Vim+ cells with a basal process was much lower (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: In TBC1D3-expressing cortices, many oRG-like cells have a basal process attaching the pial surface and without the apical process attached to the VZ surface.
source: In TBC1D3-expressing cortices, we observed many oRG-like cells with a basal process attaching the pial surface and without the apical process attached to the VZ surface (Figure 3D,F).
evidence: This is supported by DiI labeling data shown in Figure 3D,F.

claim: In control cortices, most RGs have both apical and basal processes attaching the pial and VZ surfaces respectively.
source: In the control cortices, however, most RGs had both apical and basal processes attaching the pial and VZ surfaces respectively (Figure 3D,F).
evidence: This is supported by DiI labeling data shown in Figure 3D,F.

claim: TBC1D3 expression promotes production of oRG cells, which are normally rather rare in mice.
source: Thus, TBC1D3 expression promoted production of oRG cells, which are normally rather rare in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed increase in oRG-like cells.

claim: An increase in Tbr2+ BPs is observed at 96 hr after electroporation with TBC1D3 construct at E13.5.
source: In addition, we observed an increase in Tbr2+ BPs at 96 hr after electroporation with TBC1D3 construct at E13.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F), in accordance with the linage relationship between oRG cells and IPs (Hansen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by Tbr2 staining data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: The number of cells with mitotic somal translocation (MST) is markedly higher in TBC1D3-expressing slices compared to controls.
source: In agreement with the above finding of increased oRG population, the number of cells with MST was markedly higher in TBC1D3-expressing slices, as compared to controls (Figure 3E,G).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3E,G.

claim: More than half (74/120) of proliferating cells labeled by pCAGGS-TBC1D3-IRES-EGFP are typical oRG with a single basal process and an upward MST.
source: More than half (74/120) of proliferating cells labeled by pCAGGS-TBC1D3-IRES-EGFP were typical oRG with a single basal process and an upward MST (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging and quantification data.

claim: In TBC1D3-electroporated samples, a large fraction of either apical or basal daughter cells derived from oRG cells exhibiting MST continue to express Sox2 but not Tbr2.
source: Post-imaging immunostaining of cell markers showed that, in TBC1D3-electroporated samples, a large fraction of either apical or basal daughter cells derived from oRG cells exhibiting MST continued to express Sox2 but not Tbr2 (Figure 3J–L), consistent with oRG cells with the capacity for multiple rounds of cell division.
evidence: This is supported by post-imaging immunostaining data shown in Figure 3J–L.

claim: The fraction of BrdU+EdU+ cells is higher in basal regions of TBC1D3-expressing cortices compared to controls.
source: In line with this notion, birth dating analysis using sequential labeling with BrdU and EdU showed that the fraction of BrdU+EdU+ cells was higher in basal regions of TBC1D3-expressing cortices, as compared to that of controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU/EdU double labeling data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: TBC1D3 expression in mice endows primate-like proliferative potency of oRG cells.
source: Thus, TBC1D3 expression in mice had endowed the primate-like proliferative potency of oRG cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed oRG behavior in TBC1D3-expressing mice.

claim: The primary action of TBC1D3 expression is to promote the generation of oRG cells with high proliferative capacity, leading to expansion of BPs.
source: Taken together, these results show that the primary action of TBC1D3 expression is to promote the generation of oRG cells with high proliferative capacity, leading to expansion of BPs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: TBC1D3 siRNA (siTBC1D3-440) down-regulates the expression of TBC1D3 in cultured Hela cells.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, the constructs encoding TBC1D3 siRNAs (1033, 3B, or 440) down-regulated the expression of TBC1D3 in cultured Hela cells in various degrees with siTBC1D3-440 exhibiting most effective effect.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Electroporated cells in control human brain slice samples exhibit normal delamination and a large fraction translocate to SVZ regions with typical morphology of oRG cells.
source: After culture for 72 hr, we found that electroporated cells in control samples exhibited normal delamination and a large fraction of them translocated to SVZ regions with typical morphology of oRG cells, whereas majority of siTBC1D3-electroporated cells remained in VZ regions (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data from human brain slice cultures.

claim: Majority of siTBC1D3-electroporated cells in human brain slices remain in VZ regions.
source: After culture for 72 hr, we found that electroporated cells in control samples exhibited normal delamination and a large fraction of them translocated to SVZ regions with typical morphology of oRG cells, whereas majority of siTBC1D3-electroporated cells remained in VZ regions (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data from human brain slice cultures.

claim: TBC1D3 is critical for the generation of oRG cells in human brain.
source: These results suggest that TBC1D3 is critical for the generation of oRG cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the siRNA knockdown results in human brain slices.

claim: Basal cells positive for Sox2 are markedly decreased in siTBC1D3-expressing human brain slice samples.
source: In line with this notion, basal cells positive for Sox2, which largely represents oRG cells (Pollen et al., 2015; Thomsen et al., 2016), were also markedly decreased in siTBC1D3-expressing samples (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is supported by Sox2 staining data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Co-expression with TBC1D3 largely rescues the defect caused by TBC1D3 down-regulation in human brain slices.
source: This effect was unlikely caused by off-target effect of siTBC1D3, because co-expression with TBC1D3 largely rescued the defect caused by TBC1D3 down-regulation (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Transfection with TBC1D3 siRNA markedly increases stability of Cdh2 mRNA in human neural progenitor ReNeuron cells.
source: In agreement with the result that TBC1D3 destabilized Cdh2 transcript, we found that transfection with TBC1D3 siRNA markedly increased stability of Cdh2 mRNA in human neural progenitor ReNeuron cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by mRNA stability assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: TBC1D3 plays a critical role in the generation of BPs during human brain development.
source: Taken together, TBC1D3 plays a critical role in the generation of BPs during human brain development.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the human brain slice experiments.

claim: About one third of mice electroporated with TBC1D3 construct at E13.5 show apparent folding of the cortex at P3.
source: We found that about one third of mice electroporated with the TBC1D3 construct in neuroprogenitors at E13.5 showed apparent folding of the cortex at regions containing electroporated cells when observed three days postnatal (P3) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At P7, the cortical folding induced by TBC1D3 is more pronounced than at P3.
source: At P7, the cortical folding was more pronounced (Figure 5A), suggesting a cumulative effect of TBC1D3 on the formation of gyrus-like cortical folding in mice.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The cortical surface 48 hr after electroporation shows continuous signals of laminin in both control and TBC1D3-electroporated samples.
source: The cortical surface 48 hr after electroporation showed continuous signals of laminin in both control and TBC1D3-electroporated samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), largely excluding the possibility that the later observed cortical folding might be attributed to the disruption of pial basement membrane.
evidence: This is supported by laminin staining data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: TBC1D3 transgenic mice show apparent protrusion of layer 2/3 cells towards the pial surface beginning from E14.5.
source: Beginning from E14.5, we observed apparent protrusion of layer 2/3 cells towards the pial surface in the cortex of all TG mice examined (Figure 5B,C; arrows), clear folding of cortical surface could be discerned on cortical surfaces or slices with Nissl staining in P3.5 and in adult mice (Figure 5D–F; asterisks and arrows).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Clear folding of cortical surface can be discerned in TG mice at P3.5 and in adult mice.
source: Beginning from E14.5, we observed apparent protrusion of layer 2/3 cells towards the pial surface in the cortex of all TG mice examined (Figure 5B,C; arrows), clear folding of cortical surface could be discerned on cortical surfaces or slices with Nissl staining in P3.5 and in adult mice (Figure 5D–F; asterisks and arrows).
evidence: This is supported by Nissl staining data shown in Figure 5D–F.

claim: The TG cortex shows clear lamination with Cux1 and Ctip2 markers but exhibits gyrus-like folding.
source: Immunostaining of Cux1 and Ctip2, markers for layer 2/3 and layer 5 cortical neurons, respectively, showed clear lamination in the cortex of both control and TG mice, but the TG cortex showed gyrus-like folding (Figure 5C,G).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5C,G.

claim: Cortical folding in TG mice is unlikely due to neuronal migration defects.
source: We did not observe apparent difference in vertical distribution of new born cortical neurons in TG mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), suggesting that cortical folding was unlikely due to neuronal migration defects.
evidence: This is inferred from the normal neuronal distribution pattern observed.

claim: All P3.5 TG mice examined exhibit gyrus-like phenotypes in various degrees.
source: Gross observation showed that all P3.5 TG mice examined exhibited gyrus-like phenotypes in various degrees (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by gross observation data.

claim: Gyrus-like structures in TG mice are mainly distributed in the primary (M1) and secondary (M2) motor cortex.
source: Analysis for whole-brain serial sections showed that these gyrus-like structures were mainly distributed in the primary (M1) and secondary (M2) motor cortex (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B–E).
evidence: This is supported by serial section analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4B–E.

claim: The localized effect of cortical folding may be attributed to temporal restriction of TBC1D3 expression in RG cells of TG mice and the rostral-to-caudal temporal progression of neurogenesis.
source: This localized effect may be attributed to temporal restriction of TBC1D3 expression in RG cells of TG mice and the rostral-to-caudal temporal progression of neurogenesis observed in several mammalian species (Caviness et al., 1995; McSherry and Smart, 1986; Rakic, 1974).
evidence: This is speculation based on known patterns of neurogenesis and TBC1D3 expression.

claim: At E12.5, TG mice exhibit an increase in proliferating PH3+ BPs with a wide distribution across basal regions of the cortex.
source: At E12.5, the TG mice exhibited an increase in proliferating PH3+ BPs, with a wide distribution across basal regions of the cortex, whereas only a single distinct layer contained PH3+ cells in control mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by PH3 staining data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: TG mice show a marked increase in the population of Sox2+Pax6+Tbr2- cells in basal regions.
source: More strikingly, we observed a marked increase in the population of Sox2+Pax6+Tbr2- cells in basal regions (Figure 6A,B) and more than half of them exhibited typical morphology of oRG cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: More than half of Sox2+Pax6+Tbr2- cells in TG mice exhibit typical morphology of oRG cells.
source: More strikingly, we observed a marked increase in the population of Sox2+Pax6+Tbr2- cells in basal regions (Figure 6A,B) and more than half of them exhibited typical morphology of oRG cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Some of the basal Sox2+Tbr2- cells in TG mice exhibit clustered distribution.
source: Similar to that observed in electroporation experiment (see Figure 1E), some of the basal Sox2+Tbr2- cells exhibited clustered distribution (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6F,G.

claim: Clustered columns of Sox2+Pax6+Tbr2- cells are observed beneath regions of protrusion at E14.5 in TG mice.
source: Notably, clustered columns of Sox2+Pax6+Tbr2- cells were observed beneath regions of protrusion (as defined by DAPI staining of cells) at E14.5 (Figure 6H), supporting the ontogeny unit hypothesis for cortex expansion (Rakic, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Sequential labeling with BrdU and EdU shows an increase in the number of EdU+BrdU+ basal progenitors in TG mice.
source: Sequential labeling with BrdU and EdU for mice at E13.5 and E16.5 also showed an increase in the number of EdU+BrdU+ basal progenitors in TG mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU/EdU double labeling data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Many HOPX+ cells are observed in basal extra-VZ regions of TG mice, whereas these cells are barely detectable in WT control mice.
source: Interestingly, many HOPX+ cells were observed in basal extra-VZ regions of TG mice, whereas these cells were barely detectable in WT control mice (Figure 6I,J).
evidence: This is supported by HOPX immunostaining data shown in Figure 6I,J.

claim: TBC1D3 expression promotes generation of oRG cells in mice.
source: Thus, we conclude that TBC1D3 expression promotes generation of oRG cells in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence from TG mice.

claim: TG mice exhibit increased neuronal density in the motor cortex at both P3.5 and P28, particularly in layer 2/3.
source: At both P3.5 and P28, TG mice exhibited increased neuronal density in the motor cortex showing surface folding, particularly in the layer 2/3 (Cux1+), as compared to corresponding regions in WT littermates (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–E.

claim: No apparent changes in the density of GFAP+ astrocytes are observed in adult TG mice (P28).
source: In adult mice (P28), we did not observe apparent changes in the density of GFAP+ astrocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C,F).
evidence: This is supported by GFAP quantification data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C,F.

claim: TBC1D3-induced cortical expansion is mainly due to increased number of neurons rather than astrocytes.
source: These results suggest that TBC1D3-induced cortical expansion is mainly due to increased number of neurons rather than astrocytes.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential changes in neuron and astrocyte densities.

claim: TBC1D3 expression in neuroprogenitors causes a reduced expression of Trnp1 in flow cytometry-sorted cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that TBC1D3 expression in neuroprogenitors by in utero electroporation at E13.5 caused a reduced expression of Trnp1 in flow cytometry-sorted cells at E15.5, as compared to that found in control cells sorted from vehicle-electroporated mice (Figure 7A), consistent with the finding that regional down-regulation of Trnp1 expression causes cortical folding in mice (Stahl et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: TBC1D3 expression has no effect on the stability of Trnp1 mRNA.
source: Unlike the role in destabilizing Cdh2 transcript, TBC1D3 expression had no effect on the stability of Trnp1 mRNA (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by mRNA stability assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: TBC1D3 expression has no effect on the transcriptional level of Hes1, Hes5, and Numb.
source: However, we found that TBC1D3 expression had no effect on the transcriptional level of Hes1 and Hes5, effecters of Notch signaling, as well as Numb, which encodes an endocytic adaptor protein that acts as a Notch pathway inhibitor localized to the apical membrane (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 7B–D.

claim: The signals for activated phospho-ERK1/2 (pERK1/2) are elevated in TBC1D3 TG mice, mostly in VZ/SVZ regions.
source: We found that the signals for activated phospho-ERK1/2 (pERK1/2) were elevated in TBC1D3 TG mice, mostly in VZ/SVZ regions (Figure 7F,G), in line with the previous observation that TBC1D3 enhanced the ERK signaling (Wainszelbaum et al., 2008, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by pERK1/2 immunostaining data shown in Figure 7F,G.

claim: Almost all (99.1%) of Pax6+Tbr2- oRG cells in developing human cortex are positively stained by pERK1/2.
source: Notably, almost all (99.1%) of Pax6+Tbr2- oRG cells in developing human cortex were positively stained by pERK1/2 (Figure 7H,I), further supporting the role of ERK signaling in oRG proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data from human cortex shown in Figure 7H,I.

claim: The combined actions of TBC1D3 on parallel or separate cell proliferation pathways may account for the observed role of TBC1D3 in maintaining cell stemness potency.
source: The combined actions of TBC1D3 on parallel or separate cell proliferation pathways may account for the observed role of TBC1D3 in maintaining cell stemness potency.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of TBC1D3 action.

claim: TBC1D3 expression causes delamination of vRG cells through down-regulating the level of N-cadherin and Trnp1.
source: TBC1D3 expression causes delamination of vRG cells, through down-regulating the level of N-cadherin and Trnp1, and promotes proliferation of oRG-like cells by regulating cell stemness pathways, including Ras/ERK signaling.
evidence: This is a summary of the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 7J.

claim: TBC1D3 promotes proliferation of oRG-like cells by regulating cell stemness pathways, including Ras/ERK signaling.
source: TBC1D3 expression causes delamination of vRG cells, through down-regulating the level of N-cadherin and Trnp1, and promotes proliferation of oRG-like cells by regulating cell stemness pathways, including Ras/ERK signaling.
evidence: This is a summary of the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 7J.

claim: The increased generation of oRG-like cells, IP cells, and subsequently regional increase in the density of new born neurons, induces cortical folding in mice.
source: The increased generation of the oRG-like cells, the IP cells, and subsequently regional increase in the density of new born neurons, induces cortical folding in mice.
evidence: This is the proposed model shown in Figure 7J.

claim: Amplification of VZ progenitors via overexpression of β-catenin in the mouse brain leads to folding of the ventricular rather than cortical surface.
source: However, amplification of VZ progenitors via overexpression of β-catenin in the mouse brain led to the folding of the ventricular rather than cortical surface (Chenn and Walsh, 2002), and amplification of IPs only increased the brain size without inducing cortical folding in mice (Nonaka-Kinoshita et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Amplification of IPs only increases brain size without inducing cortical folding in mice.
source: However, amplification of VZ progenitors via overexpression of β-catenin in the mouse brain led to the folding of the ventricular rather than cortical surface (Chenn and Walsh, 2002), and amplification of IPs only increased the brain size without inducing cortical folding in mice (Nonaka-Kinoshita et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Recent studies have established the association between the relative abundance of oRG and the degree of cortical folding in various species.
source: Recent studies have established the association between the relative abundance of oRG and the degree of cortical folding in various species (Betizeau et al., 2013; Hansen et al., 2010; Reillo et al., 2011; Shitamukai et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Increased population of oRG in mice is accompanied with cortical fold formation.
source: In the present study, we showed that increased population of oRG in mice is accompanied with cortical fold formation, supporting the critical role of highly proliferative oRG in cortical expansion and gyrification in primates.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental observations in this study.

claim: oRG cells are derived from the ventricular RGs, presumably requiring delamination from apical anchoring.
source: It is postulated that oRG cells are derived from the ventricular RGs, presumably requiring delamination from apical anchoring (Borrell and Gotz, 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by cited literature.

claim: Loss of adherens junction proteins or breaking their linkage to the cytoskeletal belts by down-regulating RhoA has little effect on oRG generation or cortical folding.
source: However, loss of adherens junction proteins or breaking their linkage to the cytoskeletal belts by down-regulating the small GTPase RhoA (Cappello et al., 2012; Lien et al., 2006) had little effect on oRG generation or cortical folding, although apically anchored progenitor cells became delaminated.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Delamination of VZ progenitors is not sufficient for generating highly proliferative BPs.
source: Thus, delamination of VZ progenitors is not sufficient for generating highly proliferative BPs, and changes in cell cycle regulatory factors are also be required.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature and the current study's findings.

claim: A human-specific gene ARHGAP11B promotes production of basal IPs and causes cortical folding in the electroporated mouse brain.
source: Recently, a human-specific gene ARHGAP11B has been shown to promote production of basal IPs and cause cortical folding in the electroporated mouse brain (Florio et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: TBC1D3 appeared earlier than ARHGAP11B during human evolution.
source: We propose that TBC1D3, which appeared earlier than ARHGAP11B during human evolution (Florio et al., 2015; Hodzic et al., 2006; Perry et al., 2008), acts as a candidate gene that controls many other genes involved in cortex expansion and folding.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on evolutionary timing.

claim: TBC1D3 acts as a candidate gene that controls many other genes involved in cortex expansion and folding.
source: We propose that TBC1D3, which appeared earlier than ARHGAP11B during human evolution (Florio et al., 2015; Hodzic et al., 2006; Perry et al., 2008), acts as a candidate gene that controls many other genes involved in cortex expansion and folding.
evidence: This is a proposal/speculation based on the study's findings.

claim: Multiple genes underlying different or shared cellular processes associated with neurogenesis may all contribute in part to the formation of cortical folding and gyrification found in primates.
source: Multiple genes underlying different or shared cellular processes associated with neurogenesis may all contribute in part to the formation of cortical folding and gyrification found in primates.
evidence: This is a general statement about the complexity of cortical folding mechanisms.

claim: This study provides proof-of-concept that brain development can be regulated by duplicated genes during hominoid evolution.
source: This study provides proof-of-concept that the brain development can be regulated by duplicated genes during hominoid evolution.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's significance.
